rv.q: It works to please the crowd and melt your heart a little by the end, the actors raising the effect of the too-soft humour to make lines sound more sparkling than they are.
Attractive, lightweight US romcom is smart and entertaining
And, listen buddy, there’s no funnier show uptown or downtown right now.
The comedy in this performance is outstanding.
This is a brilliant production that boasts an incredible cast and electric performances under the guidance of Lyons’ mind and Zhailon Levingston’s direction.
If you happen to be in the neighbourhood, be sure to take a seat at Table 17.

They and fellow actor Michael Rishawn, the production’s lone holdover from the US, make a hearty meal out of what in essence is fairly thin gruel, roping the audience in from the start as ready participants in the fun.
This production wants you to feel good and have fun.
Table 17 knows how to get the best from its performers and creatives.
One comes away from Table 17 with a sense that no one was a villain in Jada and Dallas' breakup, a sign of a well-written conflict that Lyons ought to have explored further.
Table 17 did exactly that for me. I found myself with a smile on my face the entire time, laughing regularly and feeling my heart growing.
Table 17 may not offer any new observations about modern relationships, but it packages familiar truths with warmth, humour and considerable charm.
It is light comic fare, skilfully served and thoroughly satisfying for anyone looking for an entertaining and undemanding evening.
Definitely make a reservation and remember to ask for Table 17.

cn.t: Critics praise this charming romcom for its sharp humor and charismatic performances, particularly from leads Marisha Wallace and Jamael Westman, who bring warmth and chemistry to this crowd-pleasing story of exes reuniting over dinner.
